why: M1 has an exit condition that says the ground truth's four layers -- entity, fault, process, evidence -- must all be fillable. Nothing could check it: the schema marks the causal chain and the checkpoints optional, and the root-cause entity id is a string no code resolves. This file names the cases that have been annotated in all four layers, with the graph that answers their references, so the count is a measurement rather than a claim. It grows one case at a time; the guard reports how many of the thirty extraction samples carry one and refuses a case that is incomplete or whose references do not resolve. Every case must carry a quote in each of its four layers, and the guard requires each quote to appear verbatim in the incident text the case was annotated from: an annotation that cannot show where it came from is an opinion about the text, and the quote is the one part of it a machine can check.

The downstream payment service is a graph node because the text names it, but it carries no checkpoint: the text says its error rate did not change, which is an absence rather than a value a checkpoint can hold.

sources.why: the defect as arithmetic: the index advances by the capacity rather than by what was written, so the boundary item is consumed twice and one line per page is never reached

sources.quote: Nothing is logged and totals still match
sources.why: why the fault never becomes an error: the loop skipped an item without evaluating a condition that could fail, and the total is summed from the source list, so both the log and the aggregate are silent by construction

sources.quote: the item on the boundary is written to the current page and then skipped on the next one
sources.why: the sentence that makes the moving reading the right one: the page carries five lines of a six-line capacity, so the count of lines is the reading that can see this and it is exact rather than sampled

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `code-null-dereference-reporting`. It is the corpus's first case whose evidence layer includes a log checkpoint, and the first whose answer is a code defect visible only as a share of one route's failures: the service is healthy, its other routes answer, and no threshold on the service as a whole has a reason to fire. The chain is two hops and ends inside the system (container -> pod -> service), and the text gives no third: the caller is named only as the account. The guard that admits a null is the defect and the migration is the trigger, which is the distinction the annotation is built to keep -- a case that named the migration would be answerable by reading the deploy log instead of the code.

sources.quote: The reporting service started returning 500 on /v2/summary
sources.why: the component and the route: the failures belong to one endpoint of one service, which is what makes the answer a code path rather than a host

sources.quote: dereferencing a field the response mapper populates only when the account has an active subscription
sources.why: the defect stated as a data-flow fact: the mapper owns the field, and the code that reads it assumes a population the mapper does not always produce

sources.quote: Accounts created after the migration have the field present but null rather than absent
sources.why: why the guard never fired: it asks whether the key is missing, and after the migration the key is always there, so the branch that would have refused the value is never reached

sources.quote: Every stack trace ends in summarize() on the same line
sources.why: the reading that names the line, and the reason the case carries a log checkpoint: no metric says "a dereference", so the evidence layer would be a guess without it

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `dependency-schema-change-currency-feed`. It is the corpus's fourth L4 and its first whose three hops leave the failing service: the chain runs through the feed's container, pod and service and ends at its consumer, so a reader who stays inside the component that reports the symptom cannot reach the answer. It is also the corpus's third case in which a different component is strictly louder -- and the first where that component is the *victim*: settlement carries a 38% mismatch share while the feed's only moving reading is a field count of one unit. Both baselines therefore return settlement first. The answer is not the deploy either: the release only dates the change, and what broke was a field whose meaning moved under its own name.

sources.quote: Settlement totals were wrong by a few cents for two hours.
sources.why: the two components and the size of the symptom: a settlement defect of a few cents, which is small enough that no threshold on the settlement service has a reason to fire

sources.quote: the rate object used to carry a single rate field and now carries rate plus inverse
sources.why: the fault stated as a payload fact: the shape of one object changed, which is the object a consumer parses rather than the service that serves it

sources.quote: Settlement's parser still reads the old field, which is now rounded
sources.why: why the error is small and why it ends: the parser is unchanged and correct against the old contract, and a rounded rate is wrong by less than a cent per order

sources.quote: the feed's own status page shows the change deployed at 09:00
sources.why: the reading that dates the change to the feed rather than to the settlement: the two hours the totals disagreed are exactly the two hours the new shape was live

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `resource-disk-full-log-collector`. It is the corpus's first `disk-full` and its first whose decisive reading is a *counter that did not move* rather than a level compared with a ceiling: the derived checkpoint `retention_runs_total.post - retention_runs_total.baseline == 0` says the job that was supposed to reclaim the volume ran zero times across the window, which no capacity reading can say. The first draft used `retention_age_hours >= 24 h` and was rejected because that threshold *is* the policy -- proving the policy with the policy is circular, and the reclamation count is the only reading that still separates 'the job is behind' from 'the job is not running'. The entity layer is the pruner container because that is what stopped; the pod is where the volume filled and the service is what stopped accepting writes, so the chain is pruner -> pod -> service and a reader who stays on the service reports the symptom. The node is cited as a configuration checkpoint rather than as a chain step: twenty gigabytes is a reasonable volume, and it is the reason the fullness arrived this week rather than a cause. Two components are deliberately *not* implicated and the checkpoints say so -- the retention window is the policy the job enforces, and the node's size is the container the policy was supposed to fit into.

sources.quote: The log collector pod stopped accepting writes at 09:41.
sources.why: the pod, the time and the fact that it is a write path: the entity layer names the pod the chain passes through and dates the symptom

sources.quote: /var/lib/collector is at 100% usage
sources.why: the observed mechanism, which is what makes this `resource` and `disk-full` rather than a slow-write fault: the path is full, not slow

sources.quote: the retention job that should trim segments older than 24h has not run since the collector was rescheduled onto a node with a smaller data volume
sources.why: the two facts the chain orders: a job that stopped, and the move it stopped at -- the sentence is why the chain starts at the pruner and cites the node rather than starting at the node

sources.quote: Writes now fail with ENOSPC and the agent is dropping batches.
sources.why: the errno and the impact: the checkpoint holds `no space left on device` from the agent line, and the dropped-batch ratio is why the ticket is about lost lines rather than latency

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `resource-memory-leak-recommendation`. It is the corpus's first whose decisive reading is a **pair of counters that only mean anything together**: `cache_writes_total` moves 7,200 times across the window and `cache_evictions_total` moves zero times. Either one alone is innocent -- a cache nothing writes to evicts nothing, and a cache that writes and evicts is working -- and the pair is the only statement that entries go in and nothing comes out. The disk-full case a round earlier made the same shape from one flat counter, and this is the version that cannot be argued with: a completion that did not happen is a job that did not run, while an eviction that did not happen is a code path that does not exist. The entity layer is the application container because that is where the cache is, and the chain runs container -> pod -> service so a reader who stops at the service reports 'it keeps restarting'. Three readings exist to refuse three innocent explanations, and each is cited as a checkpoint rather than mentioned in prose: the 2Gi limit is declared as a configuration fact so that 'the limit is too small' is answered by the same number the growth stopped at; the request rate is flat at 142 rps so that 'it grew because it was asked to do more' is answered by an equality; and the nine restarts are read as a difference rather than as a state, because one restart per eight hours is the period the slope needs rather than a failure rate. The release is deliberately *not* a checkpoint: the ticket says rolling it back stops the growth, which is a fact about a deploy rather than a reading inside the window, and putting it in the evidence layer would have made the annotation cite a sentence it cannot measure.

sources.quote: The recommendation service has OOMKilled every 6 to 8 hours for three days.
sources.why: the service, the period and the fact that it has been happening for days: the entity layer names the service the chain ends at and dates the symptom rather than the cause

sources.quote: Heap dumps show the session cache growing without bound; entries are written and never evicted.
sources.why: the mechanism stated as an asymmetry -- a write path and no eviction path -- which is what makes this `memory-leak` rather than `memory-request-overcommit`, where the process grows into a limit it was never given

sources.quote: Rolling back last Tuesday's release stops the growth.
sources.why: the only sentence that names a change instead of a symptom: growth that a rollback stops is growth that a deploy started, which is why the chain begins at the container rather than at the node that killed it

sources.quote: RSS climbs from 400Mi to the 2Gi limit and the kernel kills the container.
sources.why: the two readings the checkpoints hold: a resident set that arrives at its limit, and a kill that is the kernel's decision -- the number and the actor, in one sentence

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `network-loss-payment-gateway`. It is the corpus's first whose decisive evidence is **one wire counted from both ends**: the caller's SYN retransmits climb by 8,600 while the callee's own request rate falls from 180 to 165 rps, and the pair says a packet left and was never answered. The other half of the argument is an absence that is written down as a reading: `gateway_error_ratio` is zero. A callee that received those requests and failed them would hold its request rate and raise that ratio -- which is `dependency-upstream-5xx-pricing`, one case over in this corpus -- so the zero is what separates loss from a bad answer, and a solver explaining the timeouts by a failing gateway has to explain a zero. The entity layer is the replica rather than the service because three of the four replicas are healthy and the ticket says so in the only sentence that names a repair: retries that land on another node succeed. The egress drop counter on the caller's node is cited as evidence and explicitly *not* as the root cause: a caller retransmitting into a lossy path fills its own queue, and an annotation that stopped there would have prescribed repairing the caller's interface for a fault that lives on one replica. The `L3` level is its structure -- a pod, a service and a second service, over two causal steps -- and not a judgement about how hard the question reads.

sources.quote: Roughly 8% of calls from the order service to the payment gateway time out at 3s
sources.why: both endpoints and the rate and the deadline: the entity layer names the two services the chain joins, and the three-second deadline is the number that turns a lost packet into a failed call

sources.quote: tcpdump on the client side shows SYN retransmissions; the gateway's own metrics show it received far fewer requests than the client sent
sources.why: the mechanism on both sides of one wire -- a handshake repeated and a request never admitted -- which is what makes this `network-loss` rather than `network-delay`, where the callee receives the request and its handler time stays flat

sources.quote: Retries succeed when they land on a different node.
sources.why: the sentence that makes the fault partial rather than total: a retry that chooses another replica works, so what is broken is one replica's path and not the service or its callers

sources.quote: The egress interface on the client node reports a rising drop counter
sources.why: the reading the fifth checkpoint holds, cited as a symptom of retransmission rather than as the cause -- and the reason the annotation can say why a symptom on the caller is not where the repair goes

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `network-partition-search-cluster`. It is the corpus's first where the answer is a *relationship between two healthy things* rather than a component that got worse: six nodes became two three-node clusters, each held a majority, each elected, and both kept serving. That is why the readings are what they are -- a member count of three is one side's view rather than a cluster that lost nodes, and the election counter moved by two because each half voted -- and it is why nothing paged on availability: a fork returns yesterday's answer and is believed, where a crash returns nothing and is escalated. The entity layer is the rack switch because a firmware roll is what happened, and the answer component is the cluster because the cluster is what an operator can repair -- the split is seventeen minutes of a network team's problem and a placement policy that has to outlive it. The annotation deliberately records a gap rather than hiding it: a partition has two viewpoints and `signalRef` is one name resolved case-wide, so 'what side A saw' and 'what side B saw' cannot both be series, and the second viewpoint is prose. The guard refuses two series with one name, which is the honest refusal given that name resolution, and finding 299 is where the cost of that resolution is written down.

sources.quote: The search cluster split into two sides at 03:02 and each side elected its own leader
sources.why: the cluster, the fork and the duplication of authority in one sentence, which is the entity layer's whole claim: two leaders over one cluster is the fault, and neither half is broken

sources.quote: Queries on one side returned documents that the other side had already deleted
sources.why: the mechanism as data rather than as downtime -- the two halves disagree, and the disagreement is observable in answers

sources.quote: The split healed at 03:19 when the inter-node links came back
sources.why: the end of the window is the links returning and not a repair in the application: the duration is an interval with two timestamps, which is why it is a declared fact rather than a series

sources.quote: the only upstream event was a switch firmware roll on the rack carrying the third node
sources.why: the one change in the window, and the sentence that puts the cause outside the service graph -- a switch is not a component the application owns, which is why the answer component and the root cause entity differ here

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `config-feature-flag-checkout`: the storefront is named as where the button vanished, the flag service is named as where the value is read from, the one-minute ordering (07:59 flip, 08:00 disappearance) is the text's own, and the copy-paste is the text's own explanation rather than an inference. The deployment counter and the two job definitions are the two facts the text states as absences -- 'No deploy ran' and 'the same key in both job definitions' -- and both are written as checkpoints so that a pair of zeros and a count of writers can be falsified by a later run. Nothing about request rate or error rate is annotated, because the text names neither, and the missing flat error rate is argued in the case's own reason instead of invented here.

sources.quote: from the storefront for all users at 08:00
sources.why: the service whose rendering changed -- the answer component, and the place an operator would first look

sources.quote: a copy-paste left the same key in both job definitions
sources.why: the mechanism: not a wrong value chosen by a person but one key owned by two jobs, which is what makes the flip possible at all

sources.quote: flipped to false at 07:59 by a scheduled job that was supposed to flip a different flag
sources.why: the ordering and the actor: the flip precedes the disappearance, and it was a scheduled job rather than a deploy or a request

sources.quote: No deploy ran
sources.why: the absence the deployment counter holds; it is the one sentence that turns the most common explanation into a reading that can be false

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `dependency-version-incompatibility-shipping`: the service, the rebuild and the two mechanisms are the text's own sentences, and the two numbers a reader needs -- 2.x to 3.x, and the moved retry option -- are stated there rather than inferred. The deterministic half of the text is written as two readings that agree: a start share of zero and twenty-four attempts, which is a claim a single failure could not make. The clean-namespace sentence is a control the ticket performs on itself, so it is recorded as a declared configuration fact rather than as a second metric, because a reproduction is an event and not a sample. The log line is the constructor's refusal, quoted from the sentence that says construction throws; its body is written out so that the checkpoint's phrase and the reconstructed line can be compared by a rule rather than by a reader's memory.

sources.quote: The shipping service failed to start after the image rebuild
sources.why: the service is the answer component, and the rebuild is the boundary the whole case sits on

sources.quote: the retry option moved from a top-level field into a nested policy object, so construction throws on an unknown option
sources.why: the mechanism: a field moved between major versions, which is a version incompatibility rather than a bad value or a missing dependency

sources.quote: The failure is deterministic and reproduces in a clean namespace with the same image
sources.why: the two properties that make the cause an artifact rather than an environment, both stated by the ticket and neither inferable from a single failure

sources.quote: bumped from 2.x to 3.x
sources.why: the version pair the configuration checkpoint holds: a major bump is what makes the moved option possible, and the number is the text's

cases.why: Annotated from the incident text of `runtime-container-start-notification-worker`: the component, the entrypoint's wait, the twenty seconds and the backoff are the text's own sentences, and the rollback is a control the ticket performs on itself rather than a second incident. The two zeros are kept apart on purpose. `probe_runs_total` is a counter that stops growing, which is the text's 'No probe ever runs'; `request_rate` is a count taken at the router, which is the text's 'has not served a single request'. A single 'probe ratio is zero' would have been the same reading as the corpus's crash loop and could not have carried the sentence that explains why nobody was paged. The log line is reconstructed from the sentence that says the entrypoint waits; its body names the file so that the checkpoint's phrase and the line it cites are compared by a rule rather than by memory.

sources.quote: Its container never gets past start-up
sources.why: the container is the root cause entity and the left end of the chain, and the sentence names it as the thing that stops rather than the service that suffers

sources.quote: the entrypoint waits for a file the new image no longer creates, so it exits after twenty seconds and the kubelet backs off
sources.why: the mechanism and its three numbers: a wait, a file that stopped being created, and a backoff -- which together say start failure rather than crash

sources.quote: The notification worker has not served a single request since the last rollout
sources.why: the symptom the operator sees, and the reason the case is scored on the service rather than on the container

sources.quote: No probe ever runs
sources.why: the absence that explains the missing page: a probe that is never sent cannot fail, so no probe-based alarm could have fired
